doc.title: Steve Buckingham, interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 25, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Bad producers and the producer as film director
summary: He learned from bad producers as well as great ones and likens a producer to a film director; Rowe cites Orrin Keepnews as a catalytic agent.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: So what happens if a producer comes out and maybe they played guitar once and they’re trying to tell you, you know, do it like this and they’re holding their hands out and they’re going like that. And you know that that’s not the thing to do.

Yup. Many times. I learned as much from the great producers — the bad producers — as I did from the great producers. What not to do. I could play. A lot of producers couldn’t play. But there were also some great producers who didn’t play. But oh gosh I’ve had them stand there in front of me humming something that had nothing to do with the track, the demo or the track. And you just nod and then you do it the way you know it should be done. And then you go in the control and you go, “Thanks for that input. Thanks for that direction.” Because I’ve always said a producer in music is more like a film director. You pick the location, (the studio), you pick the tech crew (your engineers), you pick the musicians, who are like bit players, and the artist is the artist, and the script is the song, the lyrics. It’s a misnomer. A music producer is more like a film director in music. That’s it in a nutshell.
I’m glad you brought that up. Orrin Keepnews described himself as a catalytic agent.
